Empirical Research Plan: “What Drives Industry Merger Waves?”

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Primary design: Difference-in-Differences (DiD) with an interaction (“dif-dif-in-dif”)  
• Unit of observation: industry-month (48 Fama-French industries, 1981–2000).  
• “Treatment” occurs when both ( i ) an industry-specific economic shock is large and ( ii ) aggregate capital liquidity is high.  
• We compare changes in the probability (or intensity) of a within-industry merger wave across four states:

  0 = no-shock & tight-liquidity (baseline)  
  1 = shock-only  
  2 = liquidity-only  
  3 = shock × liquidity (joint condition – our treatment of interest)

The interaction term is the DiD contrast: it nets out (a) pure-shock effects and (b) pure-liquidity effects, leaving the incremental effect that requires both conditions.  
• Because liquidity is common to all industries but varies over time, while shocks vary across industries and time, the design leverages cross-section × time variation, mimicking a classic “two-way fixed-effects DiD with staggered intensity.”

Secondary design (announcement returns): event-study style OLS with deal-level CARs regressed on an “in-wave” dummy plus controls and calendar-time fixed effects. 

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Outcome variables  
A. Wave_it = 1 if industry i is in an SDC-identified wave during month t (rolling 24-month window); 0 otherwise.  
B. M&A_Intensity_it = log(1 + # deals in industry i in month t).  

Treatment variables  
• Shock_it = 1 if the industry-month is in the top quartile of an aggregate shock index (first principal component of: ΔAssetSales/Assets, ΔEmpGrowth, ΔR&D/Sales, ΔROA, ΔSalesGrowth), computed from Compustat.  
• Liquidity_t = 1 if aggregate liquidity in month t is high (credit spread below 25th pctile OR real Fed Funds below 25th pctile OR market-wide Q in the top quartile). We build a normalized index; Liquidity_t = 1 when the index > 0.5 s.d. above its 1981-2000 mean.

Treatment (Shock × Liquidity)_it ≡ Shock_it · Liquidity_t.  
Control group = the three alternative states listed above.

Timing  
Shocks are updated annually, mapped to months; liquidity is monthly. No running variable – not an RDD.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel Trends: In the absence of high liquidity, industries experiencing large shocks would have followed the same trend in merger-wave likelihood as non-shocked industries.  
  Plausibility: Shocks are measured from accounting data that do not mechanically incorporate contemporaneous M&A. We will show pre-trend plots 36–12 months before liquidity episodes.

A2. Exogeneity of Liquidity: Aggregate capital-market conditions are driven by macro factors, not by any single industry’s latent restructuring demand.  
  Plausibility: With 48 industries, any one industry is tiny relative to the bond and equity markets. We also instrument liquidity with monetary-policy surprises (Bernanke-Kuttner shocks) in robustness checks.

A3. No Spillovers Across Industries: One industry’s wave does not directly suppress or trigger another’s wave within the short window.  
  Plausibility: While some overlap is possible (e.g., supplier-customer mergers), most deal activity is intra-industry and financing capacity is deep; we will test for spillovers by adding the share of neighbouring-industry waves as a control.

A4. Stable Industry Composition (SUTVA): “Treatment” status of one industry-month does not change the definition of another’s treatment.  
  Plausibility: Industry codes are fixed by Fama-French classification; entrants are absorbed by existing codes.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Endogenous shock measurement (reverse causality).  
 • Mitigation: Use lagged (t – 1) accounting changes to form Shock_it; re-estimate with shocks constructed from commodity-price changes or regulatory dummies where available.

T2. Aggregate time trends (e.g., technological epochs) confound liquidity episodes.  
 • Mitigation: Include year-month fixed effects (or flexible splines of calendar time) so identification comes from cross-industry dispersion in shocks during the same liquidity month.

T3. Heterogeneous treatment timing bias in two-way FE DiD.  
 • Mitigation: Employ the Callaway-Sant’Anna (2021) or Sun-Abraham (2021) DiD estimators that allow for staggered, non-absorbing treatment and report event-time coefficients.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)          # fast FE regressions
library(did)             # Callaway-Sant’Anna DiD
library(sandwich); library(lmtest)

# 1. Load data --------------------------------------------------------------
sdc      <- fread("sdc_ma_industry_month.csv")      # Industry-month M&A counts, wave dummy
comp     <- fread("compustat_industry_annual.csv")  # Industry accounting vars
macro    <- fread("macro_liquidity_monthly.csv")    # Credit spreads, real rates, Q
callab   <- fread("bernanke_kuttner_shocks.csv")    # For IV robustness
crsp_car <- fread("deal_level_cars.csv")            # Acquirer CARs, wave indicator

# 2. Construct variables ----------------------------------------------------
## 2a. Industry shocks (use lagged changes)
comp <- comp[order(industry, year)]
comp[, `:=`(
  d_assetsales = asset_sales/lag(total_assets) - lag(asset_sales/total_assets),
  d_emp        = emp_growth - lag(emp_growth),
  d_rd_sales   = rd_sales - lag(rd_sales),
  d_roa        = roa - lag(roa),
  d_salesgrow  = sales_growth - lag(sales_growth)
), by = industry]

# Principal component (scale vars)
shock_vars <- c("d_assetsales","d_emp","d_rd_sales","d_roa","d_salesgrow")
comp[, (shock_vars) := lapply(.SD, scale), .SDcols = shock_vars]
pc_load <- prcomp(comp[, ..shock_vars], center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE)
comp[, shock_index := as.numeric(pc_load$x[,1])]

# Assign Shock_it dummy (top quartile within-year)
comp[, shock_dummy := shock_index > quantile(shock_index, .75, na.rm=TRUE), by = year]

## 2b. Liquidity index
macro[, `:=`(
  spread_z = scale(ig_hy_spread),
  realrate_z = scale(real_ffr),
  q_z = scale(mkt_q)
)]
macro[, liq_index := -spread_z - realrate_z + q_z]   # Higher = looser
macro[, liquidity := liq_index > quantile(liq_index, .75, na.rm=TRUE)]

# 2c. Merge industry*month panel
panel <- merge(sdc, macro, by = c("year","month"))
panel <- merge(panel, comp[,.(industry, year, shock_dummy)], 
               by = c("industry","year"), all.x = TRUE)

panel[, treat := shock_dummy * liquidity]

# 3. Main DiD regression ----------------------------------------------------
feols_res <- feols(wave ~ shock_dummy + liquidity + treat | 
                   industry + year_month, data = panel, 
                   cluster = ~industry)

summary(feols_res)

# Alternative: Callaway-Sant’Anna staggered DID ----------------------------
cs_data <- panel[ , .(industry, time_id = .GRP, treat, wave), 
                  by = .(industry, year_month)]
cs_out  <- att_gt(yname="wave", tname="time_id", idname="industry",
                  gname="treat", data=cs_data, panel=TRUE)
summary(cs_out)

# 4. Robustness: instrument liquidity with monetary-policy surprises --------
# First stage
panel <- merge(panel, callab, by=c("year","month"))
fs <- feols(liquidity ~ mp_surprise | year_month + industry, data = panel, 
            cluster = ~industry)
summary(fs)

# Second stage
iv_res <- feols(wave ~ shock_dummy + fittable(fs) + treat | 
                industry + year_month, data = panel, cluster = ~industry)
summary(iv_res)

# 5. Announcement return regression ----------------------------------------
event_res <- feols(CAR_[-1,1] ~ in_wave + controls | year_month + industry, 
                   data = crsp_car, cluster = ~acquirer_id)
summary(event_res)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
• Main prediction: β₃ (Shock × Liquidity) > 0 — industries facing a large economic shock translate that latent restructuring need into an actual merger wave only when capital markets are liquid.  
Magnitude: back-of-the-envelope, moving from state 0 to state 3 should raise the probability of a 24-month wave from ~5 % to ~15 % (10 ppt).  

• Announcement returns: CARs for in-wave deals 50–100 bp lower than otherwise comparable out-of-wave deals, consistent with greater adverse-selection or herding.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DiD)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
C1 (Parallel trends visually supported) ...................................... 1  
C2 (No anticipatory effects) ................................................ 1  
C3 (No spillovers / SUTVA) .................................................. 0.5  
C4 (Exogenous liquidity; no simultaneity) ................................... 0.5  
C5 (Proper standard errors & multiple-period DiD estimator) ................. 1  

Total = 4.0 / 5.
